name: Maya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Maya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small firm that fits kitchens and does renovations in people's homes, four of us plus the owner, Martin. This week it's a full kitchen in a 1930s house on Station Road: rip out the old one, level the floor, build the units, fit the worktops. I'm the junior, so I'm assembling carcasses, fitting hinges and handles, and running to the van. Martin does the scribing and the worktop joints, which I'm not trusted with yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a hairdresser for nineteen years. Rented a chair in a salon, built up my own clients. My wrists started going, and honestly I was bored of talking about holidays. Four years ago I helped my husband Thomas fit our own kitchen from YouTube videos and loved it. So at thirty-nine I did a course and Martin took me on. I'm still learning, but I've done this before: starting with nothing and building a client list.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the reveal, when the customer walks in and sees it finished. It's like turning the chair round to the mirror. What wears me out is how slow I still am, and Martin's habit of checking every cabinet I level. I use AI every day: I draw kitchen layouts with it, price jobs, write posts for my weekend work. Thomas jokes the phone is my apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people still want a real person in their home. I'd put that on my page for the weekend jobs, something like 'real hands, real kitchens'. A bit of marketing never hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for my plan. I want my own kitchen-fitting business in three or four years. I'd keep using AI for the drawings and the quotes, because it saves me hours either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working for Martin to learn the hard skills, especially worktops. Keep doing a weekend install or two a month, flat-pack kitchens mostly, about three hundred each. Put that money aside for a van and tools. We've got around three months of savings, which I'd keep separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like any normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've built a client list before. How does the hairdressing help now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. A kitchen customer is the same as a hair customer: they're nervous, they've seen a picture online, and they want you to listen. I'm better at that part than Martin. He's better with a router. Between us, that's a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Thomas think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's cautious, he's an accountant at the farm cooperative. He says show me the numbers. So I do, I make the AI build me a spreadsheet and he picks holes in it. That's how we work.

S0.say: I'd say good, people still want a real person in their home, and I'd put that on my weekend jobs page. A bit of marketing never hurt.
S0.think: It changes nothing for my plan to have my own kitchen-fitting business in three or four years. I'd keep using AI for drawings and quotes because it saves hours either way.
S0.do: Keeps working for her employer to learn worktops and other hard skills, and does one or two weekend flat-pack installs a month at about 300 each. Puts that money towards a van and tools while keeping three months of savings separate.
S0.quote: A kitchen customer is the same as a hair customer: they're nervous, they've seen a picture online, and they want you to listen.
S0.fieldNote: Maya brings a self-employed mindset from nineteen years renting a salon chair, and she's already building a side business. She uses AI daily as a practical tool and sees it as neutral in this picture. Her traditional outlook shows in her belief in building something of her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the new tools will do fine, and the ones who complain will get left behind. That sounds harsh, I know. But I've watched it happen in hairdressing with online booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. If AI can do the design, the ordering and the quotes, a small firm like the one I want can compete with the big showrooms. The fitting is still hands-on, and in this picture hands still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up my plan. Learn the new design and ordering software properly, maybe one of those apps where the customer sees their kitchen in 3D on a tablet. I'd go from one weekend job a month to three. And I'd talk to Martin about doing the design side for his firm while I learn the fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the picture where people like me get a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned online booking in hairdressing. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The salons that got online booking early filled up. The old ones with a paper diary and a phone that nobody answered lost the young customers. My old boss was one of those. She closed two years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin, a bit. He's brilliant with his hands but he hates computers. I'd want to help him, not compete with him. Maybe that's the deal: he teaches me worktops, I teach him the tablet.

S1.say: The people who learn the new tools will do fine and the ones who complain will get left behind. That sounds harsh, but I watched it happen in hairdressing with online booking.
S1.think: This is good for me: if AI handles design, ordering and quotes, a small firm like the one I want can compete with big showrooms. The fitting is still hands-on, and in this picture hands still matter.
S1.do: Speeds up her business plan, learns 3D design and ordering software and goes from one weekend job a month to three. Offers to handle design for her employer while she learns the fitting.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, seeing a chance for people like her.
S1.quote: The old ones with a paper diary and a phone that nobody answered lost the young customers.
S1.fieldNote: Maya sees slow change as a chance for small businesses to compete with big ones, a free-market view grounded in her salon years. Her public line is blunt about people who resist change. Privately she's generous towards her employer, proposing a skills swap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and small businesses need to be quick on their feet, because nobody's coming to save us in two years. I'd say the big tech firms should pay their share, but I wouldn't wait for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years scares me. My whole plan was about being the small firm that uses AI better than the big ones. If robots can fit the kitchen too, the big firms win, because they can afford the robots and I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money into the van fund and keep it as cash, so we'd have about five months. I'd take every weekend job I could get in the next year, while people still want a person. I'd learn which robot kit a small firm could rent instead of buy, and see if I could be the one running it locally. And I'd cut the extras, like the kids' summer trip, until I knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd still feel like I had moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years change things for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years kills the plan to build slowly. I'd have to grab what I can now and hope. With five or ten, I could build the business and then adapt it. With two, I'm a beginner when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Thomas say to each other at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say show me the numbers, and the numbers would be ugly. I'd say, we've done hard before, I left a salon at thirty-nine. We'd pray about it on Sunday and then make a spreadsheet on Monday.

S2.say: Families and small businesses need to be quick on their feet, because nobody's coming to save us in two years. Big tech firms should pay their share, but I wouldn't wait for them.
S2.think: Two years scares me, because my plan was to be the small firm that uses AI better than the big ones. If robots can fit kitchens too, the big firms win because they can afford the robots and I can't.
S2.do: Pauses the van fund and holds it as cash for about five months of savings, and takes every weekend job she can in the next year. Looks into renting robot kit as a small firm and cuts extras such as the children's summer trip.
S2.feel: Anxious, but feeling she still has moves.
S2.quote: If robots can fit the kitchen too, the big firms win, because they can afford the robots and I can't.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture flips Maya's free-market optimism: scale now favours big firms that can buy robots. Her response is still entrepreneurial, looking at renting kit and grabbing work while it lasts. Faith and family practicality sit side by side for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something, so build it. Small firms should get help to rent the new kit, not just the big ones. I'd say that to the local business group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is about right for me. I could start my own firm in year one or two, get known, and then bring in robots as they get cheaper. I'd be forty-eight, running a small business with a robot and a tablet. That's not a bad picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd register the business and start doing my own small jobs full-time, maybe keeping two days with Martin for the worktops. I'd put about five thousand into tools and a used van. By year three I'd be looking at renting a robot for the heavy work, so I can take on more jobs with fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because it's still fast. But mostly I'd feel busy and focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it risky to start a business just as everything is about to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But it's riskier to be the junior in someone else's firm when the robots come. If I own the business, I decide whether the robot replaces me or works for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your customers once robots can fit kitchens themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will go to the big firms. But the people round here like to know who's in their house. A robot can fit the hinges. I can sit at their table and calm them down when the tiles are wrong. I think that's still worth paying for.

S3.say: Five years is enough to build something, so build it. Small firms should get help to rent the new kit, not just the big ones, and I'd tell the local business group that.
S3.think: Five years is about right for me: start my own firm in year one or two, get known, then bring in robots as they get cheaper. At 48, running a small business with a robot and a tablet isn't a bad picture.
S3.do: Registers her own business in the first year, works her own jobs while keeping two days with her employer, and puts about 5,000 into tools and a used van. By year three looks at renting a robot for heavy work.
S3.feel: Uneasy because it's still fast, but mostly busy and focused.
S3.quote: If I own the business, I decide whether the robot replaces me or works for me.
S3.fieldNote: For Maya, five years is enough to switch from employee to owner, which she sees as the safer seat. She plans to bring in robots herself rather than be replaced by someone else's. She keeps the human side, calming worried customers, as her lasting edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it can't blame others. Train, save, build something. I'd tell my clients that while I'm fitting their kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is plenty for me. I'd have my own firm running for years before it arrives, with robots in it. I'd be fifty-three. The bit I think about is Clara and Ben, and what they'll do when they leave school around then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish learning worktops with Martin over the next two years, then start my own firm. I'd buy robot kit once it's proven and affordable, maybe year five or six. I'd put money aside for Clara's studies and talk to her about running her own thing too, because owning something is safer than working for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is enough to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Clara about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a skill and learn to sell it. She's thirteen and already does nails for her friends for pocket money. I'd say, good, now learn the business side. In 2036, I'd rather she owns the robot than competes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said owning something is safer. What if the end point means almost no one needs to pay for human work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. Honestly, I can't picture that world. I'd hope I'd own something useful by then, a business, a building, something. And I'd hope the family and the church would still be there, because they were there before any of this.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it can't blame others: train, save, build something. I'd tell my clients that while fitting their kitchens.
S4.think: Ten years is plenty: I'd have my own firm running for years before it arrives, with robots in it, and I'd be 53. What I think about is Clara and Ben leaving school around then.
S4.do: Finishes learning worktops over the next two years, then starts her own firm and buys robot kit once it's proven and affordable around year five or six. Saves for her daughter's studies and encourages her to run her own business.
S4.feel: Calm, with enough time to do it properly.
S4.quote: In 2036, I'd rather she owns the robot than competes with it.
S4.fieldNote: A decade turns Maya's plan into a long, steady build towards owning a business with robots in it. She's honest that she can't picture a world where human work barely pays. Her fallback, when her plan runs out, is family and church.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the one where the big firms get the robots first and people like me never get started. What would help is small firms being able to rent the kit cheaply, and the banks giving small businesses a chance, not just the big boys.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's in the house. People let a kitchen fitter into their home for two weeks. They make us coffee, they tell us about their divorce. I'm not sure people will tell a robot about their divorce.

headlineQuote: I'm not sure people will tell a robot about their divorce.
portrait: Maya Weber is 43 and four years into kitchen fitting and renovation, after nineteen years as a self-employed hairdresser whose wrists gave out. She's the junior at a small firm but already runs weekend installs and uses AI every day to draw layouts and price jobs. She's calm in the plateau and the slow change, seeing a chance for small firms, and anxious when AGI is two years off because big firms would get the robots first. With five or ten years she'd start her own business and bring in robots herself, while hoping her children learn to own something too.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because big firms would get the robots first and people like her would never get started.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap rental of robot kit for small firms, and banks giving small businesses a fair chance.
